Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment pipeline.
We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E)
We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads.

we define three experimental conditions: Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor-Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E).
Baseline serves as a reference configuration that permits only the transformations required for NPU execution while limiting optional vendor-specific optimizations.
VG-NPU applies the vendor-guided model transformation recipe while preserving the same model inputs and outputs and the same host-side processing as Baseline.
VG-E2E applies the full vendor-recommended deployment configuration, including native input/output formats, preprocessing, runtime execution, and postprocessing.
where VG-NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline.
We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads.
First, under VG-NPU, both latency and accuracy improve in 10 of the 12 NPU–workload combinations.
In contrast, under VG-E2E, System-level latency decreases in all combinations, while accuracy decreases in eight.
and VG-E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level latency over VG-NPU.

This result shows that vendor-guided optimization can improve both metrics at the controlled model-transformation level, but that lower latency in the final deployment does not necessarily imply preserved accuracy.

Third, VG-E2E achieves lower System-level latency than VG-NPU in all combinations. This suggests that deployment-level processing can provide additional performance gains, while also indicating that such gains should not be attributed to any single optimization component.
